## Stated limitations

Coverage claims are only as strong as the telemetry they depend on. These limitations are part of the control statement, not footnotes.

### Suspicious Process Access to LSASS Memory

**Depth:** medium. Access-mask based and resistant to tool renaming; blind to handle duplication and unlisted masks

**Depends on:**
- Sysmon Event ID 10 (ProcessAccess) with an include rule for TargetImage lsass.exe

**Known blind spots:**
- Handle duplication from another process never opens LSASS directly
- Access masks outside the listed values
- Code injected into a named Windows component (csrss, wininit, WmiPrvSE) - its CallTrace shows a frame with no module (UNKNOWN)
- Credential Guard / RunAsPPL environments where the real control is prevention
- ProcessAccess telemetry disabled or filtered for volume

### Suspicious Child Process of a WinRM Session Host

**Depth:** medium. Shells, encoded PowerShell and five proxy binaries under both WinRM hosts; blind to cmdlet-only sessions and custom binaries

**Depends on:**
- Sysmon Event ID 1 (ProcessCreate) on the WinRM target - the generated KQL and SPL read Sysmon; Security 4688 works only after remapping NewProcessName and ParentProcessName in tools/mappings.yml, and has no OriginalFileName

**Known blind spots:**
- Commands that run as cmdlets inside wsmprovhost.exe start no child process
- Binaries outside the listed shells and proxies (custom tools copied to the target)
- WMI and DCOM remote execution, which run under WmiPrvSE.exe and other hosts

### Crontab Installed From Standard Input or a File

**Depth:** partial. Non-interactive crontab installs only; direct writes to cron files and systemd timers are not covered

**Depends on:**
- Sysmon for Linux Event ID 1 (ProcessCreate) - the generated KQL reads the SysmonForLinux parser function and the SPL reads sourcetype sysmon:linux; auditd EXECVE carries the same arguments but needs its own mapping in tools/mappings.yml

**Known blind spots:**
- Writing the spool file (/var/spool/cron) or /etc/cron.d directly, without the crontab binary - a file-event rule covers it
- systemd timers and at jobs, which are other persistence mechanisms
- crontab -e driven by a script that sets EDITOR to a non-interactive command

### Scheduled Task Registered via PowerShell ScheduledTasks Cmdlets

**Depth:** partial. Command-line cmdlet usage only; script files and COM API require 4104 and 4698

**Depends on:**
- Sysmon Event ID 1 (ProcessCreate) - the generated KQL and SPL read Sysmon; Security 4688 works only after remapping NewProcessName and ParentProcessName in tools/mappings.yml, and has no OriginalFileName
- PowerShell Script Block Logging 4104 (catches cmdlets inside scripts)
- Security 4698

**Known blind spots:**
- Cmdlets executed inside a .ps1 file never appear on the command line (needs 4104)
- Tasks registered from XML definitions
- COM API (Schedule.Service) task creation

### Scheduled Task Created With Suspicious Action

**Depth:** partial. schtasks.exe command lines only; PowerShell is covered by a separate rule, COM API is not covered

**Depends on:**
- Sysmon Event ID 1 (ProcessCreate) - the generated KQL and SPL read Sysmon; Security 4688 works only after remapping NewProcessName and ParentProcessName in tools/mappings.yml, and has no OriginalFileName
- Security 4698 (recommended, holds the task XML)

**Known blind spots:**
- Tasks created through the COM API or PowerShell cmdlets without schtasks.exe
- Task XML written directly to the Tasks folder and TaskCache registry
- Benign task path that runs a malicious script

### PowerShell Execution With Encoded Command

**Depth:** medium. Defeats parameter abbreviation, -- / Unicode-dash prefixes, quoting around the switch or blob, and renaming; blind to non-encoded obfuscation and hosted runspaces

**Depends on:**
- Sysmon Event ID 1 (ProcessCreate) - the generated KQL and SPL read Sysmon; Security 4688 works only after remapping NewProcessName and ParentProcessName in tools/mappings.yml, and has no OriginalFileName
- PowerShell Script Block Logging 4104 (recommended, holds the decoded script)

**Known blind spots:**
- Payload passed through stdin or environment variables
- Obfuscation inside a non-encoded command
- PowerShell hosted inside another process (System.Management.Automation.dll)
- Quotes inside the switch name or the Base64 blob (-e"nc", -enc "VwBy"AGkA...) - argv parsing strips them, so PowerShell still runs the payload; 4104 script block logging covers the decoded script

### Linux Shell Executing Decoded Base64 or Code From a Temporary Directory

**Depth:** medium. Decoded Base64 piped into a shell through -c, binaries in three temporary directories, and shell scripts started from them

**Depends on:**
- Sysmon for Linux Event ID 1 (ProcessCreate) - the generated KQL reads the SysmonForLinux parser function and the SPL reads sourcetype sysmon:linux; auditd EXECVE carries the same arguments but needs its own mapping in tools/mappings.yml

**Known blind spots:**
- A pipeline typed in an interactive shell runs base64 and sh as separate processes with no shared command line
- Interpreters other than shells (python, perl) running code from temporary directories
- Temporary directories outside /tmp, /var/tmp and /dev/shm, such as a user's ~/.cache

### Windows Event Log Clearing via Command Line

**Depth:** medium. Command-line methods; the 1102 and 104 rules cover the outcome regardless of method

**Depends on:**
- Sysmon Event ID 1 (ProcessCreate) - the generated KQL and SPL read Sysmon; Security 4688 works only after remapping NewProcessName and ParentProcessName in tools/mappings.yml, and has no OriginalFileName

**Known blind spots:**
- Clearing through Event Viewer or the Win32 API from a custom binary
- Selective event deletion or killing EventLog threads
- Clearing performed remotely (wevtutil /r:host) logs the process on the source, not the target

### Security Audit Log Cleared (Event 1102)

**Depth:** high. Outcome-based: fires whenever the Security log is cleared, by any method

**Depends on:**
- Security Event ID 1102

**Known blind spots:**
- Attackers who stop the EventLog service or tamper with forwarding before clearing
- Only the Security log; other logs are covered by System 104
- Hosts whose Security log is not forwarded before the clear leave no copy to investigate

### Windows Event Log Cleared (System Event 104)

**Depth:** high. Outcome-based: fires whenever a non-Security log is cleared, including Sysmon and PowerShell

**Depends on:**
- System Event ID 104 (Microsoft-Windows-Eventlog)

**Known blind spots:**
- EventLog service stopped or forwarding tampered with before clearing
- Security log clearing (covered by 1102)
- Logs cleared by stopping the service and deleting .evtx files produce no 104 event

### Rundll32 Proxy Execution From Suspicious Context

**Depth:** medium. Four distinct abuse patterns; blind to malicious DLLs placed in trusted paths

**Depends on:**
- Sysmon Event ID 1 (ProcessCreate) - the generated KQL and SPL read Sysmon; Security 4688 works only after remapping NewProcessName and ParentProcessName in tools/mappings.yml, and has no OriginalFileName

**Known blind spots:**
- DLL copied into System32 before execution
- Malicious DLL in a trusted path called by ordinal
- rundll32 without arguments only matches if the command line is captured exactly
- A writable folder reached through its 8.3 short name (C:\PROGRA~3\...) - the path branch reads long names only (public data, EVTX-ATTACK-SAMPLES rundll32_cmd_schtask)

### Run Key Persistence Pointing to Suspicious Location

**Depth:** partial. Run and RunOnce keys only; other autostart extensibility points need their own rules

**Depends on:**
- Sysmon Event ID 13 (RegistryEvent value set) with includes for Run and RunOnce keys

**Known blind spots:**
- Other autostart locations (Winlogon, IFEO, Startup folder, UserInitMprLogonScript)
- Payload placed in a trusted path (DLL side-loading)
- Offline hive edits

### Kerberoasting - RC4 Service Ticket Requested for User Account

**Depth:** medium. Single-event RC4 rule plus aggregation and contextual hunts in queries/hunts

**Depends on:**
- Security Event ID 4769 on domain controllers (Audit Kerberos Service Ticket Operations)

**Known blind spots:**
- AES ticket requests (Rubeus /aes) - the rule sees only RC4; queries/hunts/kerberoasting_volume_hunt counts every encryption type
- Low-and-slow roasting of a single account
- Roasting run on a domain controller - tickets requested from ::1 are filtered with the DC's own service traffic
- Domains where RC4 is still common

### Suspicious Service Installation (PsExec-style / Command Services)

**Depth:** medium. Fingerprints PsExec, Impacket psexec and smbexec plus generic command services; blind to service modification

**Depends on:**
- System Event ID 7045 (Service Control Manager)
- Security 4697 (optional)

**Known blind spots:**
- Randomised service name with the binary placed in System32
- Modifying an existing service ImagePath (sc config) produces no 7045
- WMI, WinRM and DCOM lateral movement

### Password Spray - One Source Failing Authentication for Many Accounts

**Depth:** medium. Kerberos and NTLM failures for many accounts from one source (wrong password, unknown or disabled account), counted per 10-minute window with a proven 9-account guarantee; distributed and low-and-slow sprays need longer-window hunting

**Depends on:**
- Security Event ID 4771 on domain controllers (Audit Kerberos Authentication Service = Failure)
- Security Event ID 4768 failures on domain controllers (the same audit subcategory)
- Security Event ID 4625 on domain controllers and on member servers that accept network or RDP logons (Audit Logon = Failure)

**Known blind spots:**
- Low-and-slow sprays that stay under 5 accounts per source in every 10-minute window
- Sprays spread over many source addresses (botnets, cloud egress pools), each source below the threshold
- Sprays against cloud identity (Entra ID sign-in logs) - this correlation reads on-premises Windows events only
- NTLM failures a domain controller validates for a member server (4776) carry no client address; they are counted through the member server's own 4625, so member server Security logs must be collected
- A spray run on the host itself (logon attempts with no remote address, public data PurpleSharp local and NTLM variants) is seen only as 4776 by workstation name on the domain controller, which this correlation does not count
- A burst of 5 to 8 accounts can be split by a window boundary; 9 or more within 10 minutes always alert

### API Probing - One Client Rejected on Many Distinct Paths

**Depth:** partial. Rejected requests on many paths from one client; distributed and slow probing need longer-window hunting

**Depends on:**
- Web server or reverse-proxy access log with client address, method, path and status - the generated KQL reads W3CIISLog and the SPL reads sourcetype access_combined; other tables need their columns in tools/mappings.yml

**Known blind spots:**
- Probes spread over many client addresses (cloud egress pools, botnets), each below 5 paths
- Slow probes that stay under 5 rejected paths per client in every 5-minute window
- A reverse proxy that logs its own address instead of the client's (use X-Forwarded-For)
- A burst of 5 to 8 paths can be split by a window boundary; 9 or more within 5 minutes always alert

### Object ID Enumeration - One Client Walking Single-Owner Objects

**Depth:** partial. Numeric IDs of five single-owner object types in the path; other identifier styles and object types need the base rule edited

**Depends on:**
- Web server or reverse-proxy access log with client address, method and path - the generated KQL reads W3CIISLog and the SPL reads sourcetype access_combined; other tables need their columns in tools/mappings.yml

**Known blind spots:**
- Object IDs passed in the query string or the request body instead of the path
- Non-numeric identifiers (UUIDs, slugs)
- Object types outside the base rule's list - edit it to your application's single-owner objects
- A walk of 3 or 4 objects can be split by a window boundary; 5 or more within a minute always alert

### Kerberoasting - One Client Requesting Tickets for Many Service Accounts

**Depth:** high. Volume over every encryption type complements the RC4 single-event rule; together they cover RC4 and AES roasting, with a proven 9-account guarantee

**Depends on:**
- Security Event ID 4769 on domain controllers (Audit Kerberos Service Ticket Operations = Success)

**Known blind spots:**
- Targeted roasting of one to four service accounts per 10 minutes - covered by the RC4 single-event rule and by honeypot SPN accounts
- Roasting spread over several source addresses, each below the threshold
- AS-REP roasting (accounts without pre-authentication) produces 4768, not 4769, and is not counted here
- A burst of 5 to 8 service accounts can be split by a window boundary; 9 or more within 10 minutes always alert
